course.title: Camday – Cambridge Lower Secondary Science — Stage 7

unit.title: Electricity
unit.blurb: Electron flow, conductors and insulators, circuit diagrams and symbols, measuring current with an ammeter, and how cells and lamps change the current.

O1.t: Describe electricity as a flow of electrons and classify materials as conductors or insulators.

O2.t: Explain open and closed circuits and draw circuit diagrams using standard symbols.

O3.t: Measure current in amperes with an ammeter in series and recognise that current is the same everywhere in a series circuit.

O4.t: Predict how adding cells or lamps in series changes the current and lamp brightness.

captions: Welcome to Camday.
This lesson was written by the Camday teaching team to
help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 12: Electricity.
Electricity carries energy to our homes, schools and even cars.
Every time you press a switch, you close an electrical circuit.
How do circuits work, and how can we use electricity without wasting it?
Let's find out.
All matter is made of atoms, and atoms contain even smaller particles: protons,
neutrons and electrons. Electrons have a negative charge.
In some materials, like metals,
some electrons are free to leave their atoms and move between them.
They can be made to flow in one direction,
carrying their charge with them.
This flow of electrons is electricity.
A steel coin, a plastic ruler,
the graphite 'lead' of a pencil and a rubber eraser are placed,
one at a time, in the gap of a simple circuit.
Predict: which ones will make the lamp light?
Pause and decide.
Watch. Each material is clipped into the gap in turn.
The lamp lights with the coin, and glows dimly with the graphite.
It stays off with the plastic ruler and the rubber eraser.
Explain what you saw.
The steel coin is a metal, a good conductor with free electrons,
so current flows and the lamp lights.
Graphite is a non-metal, but it is unusual: it conducts,
though not as well as a metal.
Plastic and rubber are insulators: their electrons are not free to move,
so no current flows.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
Materials that let electrons flow through them freely are electrical conductors.
Metals such as copper,
gold and iron are good conductors because they have many free electrons.
In electrical insulators, like plastic, glass and rubber,
electrons are not free to move, so they stop electricity flowing.
On electricity pylons, glass insulators stop the current flowing
from the cables down into the metal poles.
To test a material, place it in a gap in a simple circuit.
If the lamp lights up, the material has completed the circuit,
so it is a conductor.
Here, a metal coin lights the lamp.
An electric kettle's plug and cord have metal inside to carry the current,
but they are covered in plastic, an insulator.
That's why we can touch them safely.
People who work with electricity wear insulating rubber gloves and shoes with rubber soles,
because rubber doesn't conduct electricity.
If we touch an exposed wire,
electrons can flow through our body into the ground,
giving us an electric shock.
Copper is one of the best conductors,
so it's used for wiring in buildings.
Long overhead cables use aluminium, which is cheaper and lighter.

captions: An electrical circuit is a complete path that electrons can flow around.
Energy stored in the cell is transferred electrically through the wires to the lamp.
When there is a continuous path, it's a closed circuit,
and the lamp lights up.
If there's a gap or break, electrons can't flow.
It's an open circuit, and the lamp goes out.
Flipping a light switch to off opens the circuit.
The cell drives the electrons,
and two or more cells joined together make a battery.
A switch lets us open or close the circuit whenever we want.
Every switch opens or closes a circuit.
Here are four you might use today.
In a torch, sliding the switch closes the circuit,
so current flows from the cells through the lamp.
A doorbell button is a push switch.
Pressing it closes the circuit and the bell rings;
letting go opens it again.
A fridge has a small switch in the door frame.
Opening the door closes the circuit and the light comes on.
Traffic lights use automatic switches, controlled by a timer,
to open and close the circuit for each coloured lamp.
Pause and decide: when the fridge door is shut,
is the light's circuit open or closed?
Instead of drawing real pictures, scientists draw circuit diagrams using symbols.
Here are the electrical cell, a battery of cells, a lamp,
and an open switch.
And here are a closed switch, an ammeter, a buzzer and a wire.
In the cell symbol, the long line is the positive terminal,
and the short line is the negative terminal.
Wires are drawn as straight lines.
Let's try a worked example.
A student builds a doorbell with a cell, wires and a buzzer.
What else should the circuit have?
A switch! Nobody wants a doorbell that never stops ringing.
Now draw the circuit diagram: start with the cell,
then add the buzzer and a closed switch, in any order,
and join them with straight wires.
Electricity travels incredibly fast,
so the buzzer sounds the moment you press the switch!

captions: Electric current is the flow of charge carried by electrons around a circuit.
It's measured in amperes, or amps for short, symbol A, using an ammeter.
The current tells us how much charge flows past a point every second.
Which way does current flow?
Early scientists thought it flowed from the positive terminal to the negative,
and we still call this conventional current.
But when electrons were discovered, they turned out to flow the opposite way:
from negative to positive!
A student puts three ammeters in a series circuit with a cell and two lamps:
before the first lamp, between the lamps, and after the second lamp.
All three ammeters read 0.30 amps.
Pause and decide: what does this tell you about the current in a series circuit?
Is any current used up by the lamps?
To measure the current through a component, connect the ammeter in series:
in one continuous line with it, with no branches.
The red, positive terminal of the ammeter connects towards the positive end of the cell.
Put ammeters at different points in a series circuit with several lamps,
and they all show the same reading!
The current is the same everywhere in a series circuit.
It isn't used up as it flows through each lamp.
The energy is transferred to the lamps as light and heat,
but the charge keeps flowing.

p: Early scientists decided current flows from the **positive (+)** terminal round to the **negative (−)** terminal. We still use this **conventional current**.

stops.note: Paused after: “Without gravity, astronauts' muscles lose strength, so they must exercise for hours every ”

captions: Cells provide the push that moves charges around a circuit.
Add a second cell in series, and the push is bigger,
so more current flows and the lamp shines more brightly.
But careful: too many cells can damage a lamp!
Now add a second lamp in series.
Lamps make it harder for electrons to flow.
We call this resistance.
Two lamps give more resistance, so less current flows,
and each lamp is dimmer than a single lamp.
The same cell is used each time, and one, two,
then three identical lamps are connected in series.
The current is measured each time.
With one lamp the current is 0.40 amps.
With two lamps it falls to about 0.21 amps,
and with three lamps to 0.14 amps.
The lamps also get dimmer.
Pause and decide: why does adding lamps make the current smaller?
On the International Space Station,
every room is packed with electrical circuits controlling life support and communication.
Huge solar cells absorb energy from sunlight to power them all.
Without gravity, astronauts' muscles lose strength,
so they must exercise for hours every day.
Scientists are testing electrical muscle stimulation:
controlled electric currents that make muscles work and grow stronger.
Doctors already use it to help injured and elderly patients.
Electric current can do far more than light a lamp!
Now it is your turn to shine!
Pause the video after each question and try to answer it first.
Question 1: Why are metals good electrical conductors?
Pause the video now.
Answer: They have free electrons that can move between atoms.
Question 2: What is the difference between an open and a closed circuit?
Pause the video now.
Answer: A closed circuit is a complete path so current flows;
an open circuit has a gap.
Question 3: How must an ammeter be connected?
Pause the video now.
Answer: In series, with its positive terminal towards the + end of the cell.
Question 4: What happens to the current if you add more lamps in series?
Pause the video now.
Answer: Resistance increases, so the current decreases and the lamps are dimmer.

retired.prompt: Cells provide the ___ that moves charges.
Lamps make it harder for electrons to flow. This is…

p: You have a circuit with one cell and one lamp. You can add another cell, or another lamp.
Predict what each change does to the brightness of the lamps.
Each cell gives the electrons a push. **More cells in series give a bigger push**, so **more current** flows and the lamp is **brighter**.
p2: Careful: too many cells give so much current that the lamp's filament can melt and the lamp 'blows'. Cells must be joined + to −, or they cancel each other out.

p: Components such as lamps make it harder for current to flow – they have **resistance**.
p2: **More lamps in series → more resistance → less current**, so each lamp is **dimmer** than one lamp on its own.

read.t: Real data: adding lamps in series
p: The same cell was used with one, two and then three identical lamps in series.
p2: Each extra lamp adds resistance, so the current falls – and the lamps get dimmer.

qq.prompt: A circuit has one cell and two lamps in series. A third lamp is added in series. What happens?
qq.reason: Resistance rises, current falls, every lamp is dimmer.

options.t: The current decreases and the lamps get dimmer.
The current stays the same, but the lamps get dimmer.
Only the new lamp is dim.
options.fb: In series the current is the same through all the lamps.

qq.prompt: Compared with one cell and one lamp, is the lamp brighter or dimmer?
qq.reason: More cells → more current → brighter; more lamps → less current → dimmer.

p: On the International Space Station, huge **solar panels** transfer energy from sunlight to the circuits that run life support, computers and radios.
p2: Doctors use small controlled currents to make muscles contract (**electrical muscle stimulation**) – it helps injured patients, and scientists are testing it to keep astronauts' muscles strong in space.

p: More **cells** in series → more current → brighter lamps.
More **lamps** in series → more **resistance** → less current → dimmer lamps.
Electricity powers spacecraft through solar panels and can help muscles in medicine.
